text: Aaron Leo Brody (August 23, 1930 – July 26, 2021) was an American food scientist known for developing innovations in food processing and packaging. He created the first frozen fish sticks in the 1950s and, while working at Mars, Incorporated, introduced Starburst to the United States. Brody was born in Boston, Massachusetts, as the elder of two children to Nathan Brozozek and Lillian Gorman, Jewish immigrants from Poland; his father’s name was Americanized to Brody upon entry through Ellis Island. He attended Solomon-Lewenburgh Junior High School and then Boston English School in 1947. Brody entered the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1947, earning a B.S. in Food Technology in 1951. He worked as an illustrator for the MIT school newspaper, primarily using pen on paper to depict sports figures. He was drafted into the Korean War and served from 1952 to 1954 at Fort Pickett in Blackstone, Virginia, where he reported on wounded soldiers returning from the war as a newspaper correspondent. After his military service, he pursued a graduate degree in the Food Packaging Department at MIT, earning a Ph.D. in 1957 under Bernard E. Proctor, a prominent food scientist involved in early food irradiation research and the chair of the MIT Food Technology Department. His work, "Masticatory Properties of Foods by the Strain Gage Denture Tenderometer," was featured in Life magazine on October 29, 1956, with a full-page illustration of the machine chewing mozzarella cheese; the device is on display at the MIT Museum and enabled food manufacturers to control product qualities for process design. Brody later earned an M.B.A. from Northeastern University in 1970. While still in school, he began working at the Birdseye Fisheries Lab Division of General Foods in 1951, contributing to the development of the first frozen precooked foods, including fish sticks. As a graduate student, he worked part-time at Raytheon Manufacturing Company, where he helped develop the first microwave oven, enabling microwave cooking, heating, and browning of foods. After completing his graduate studies, he joined the Whirlpool Corporation in Benton Harbor, Michigan, where he led the development of modified atmosphere packaging (MAP), invented an odor control system for refrigerators, a thermoelectric refrigerator/freezer, the Total Environmental Control “Tectrol” controlled atmosphere process for food preservation, a progenitor of MAP for fresh-cut vegetables, and radiation pasteurization of foods. He also patented an apparatus and method for storing perishable animal and plant materials, as well as non-food materials. At Mars, Inc.’s M&M Candies Division, Brody developed commercial confectionery products including Starburst and Pop Rocks; his team adapted the British candy Opal Fruits into M&M Fruit Chewies, which were later renamed Starburst due to the connotation of M&M’s with chocolate. At Mead Packaging, he invented the Crosscheck Aseptic Packaging System for high-acid fluid foods like juices and sauces, receiving patents US4,152,464, US4,391,080, and US4,409,775. At Container Corporation of America, he led the development of the Versaform insert injection molding system and served as Marketing Development Manager, his final corporate role. By the mid-1980s, Brody transitioned into independent consulting and teaching, offering courses in food packaging and product development and marketing at The University of Georgia, MBA strategic marketing and product development at Saint Joseph's University, and packaging courses at Michigan State University. He authored numerous articles and ten textbooks on food packaging, food technology, marketing, and packaging, including The Encyclopedia of Packaging Technology, which covers packaging technologies across industries from food to automobiles, soft drinks to pharmaceuticals, and Modified Atmosphere Packaging for Fresh-Cut Fruits and Vegetables, which details modern MAP technologies for fresh-cut fruits. Brody married Carolyn Goldstein on April 11, 1953, and remained married until her death in April 2021; they had three children. He died on July 26, 2021, from congestive heart failure. In 1964, he received the Industrial Achievement Award from the Institute of Food Technologists and the Leadership Award from the Packaging Institute. He was named Packaging Man of the Year in 1985 by the National Association of Packaging, Handling, and Logistics Engineers. In 1988, the Food Packaging Division of the Institute of Food Technologists awarded him the Riester-Davis Award for Lifetime Achievement in Food Packaging, the highest industry honor in the field. In 1994, he was the first recipient of the Institute of Food Technologists' Industrial Scientist Award for technical contributions to the food industry. In 1995, he was inducted into the Packaging Hall of Fame. In 2000, he received the Nicholas Appert Award from the Institute of Food Technologists for his lifetime contributions. The Michigan State School of Packaging established the Annual Aaron Brody Distinguished Lecture in Food Packaging as an endowment created by family and friends in recognition of his lifelong achievements. In 2015, the Food Packaging Division of the Institute of Food Technologists renamed the Riester-Davis Award to the Riester-Davis-Brody Award in his honor. Brody was quoted in The New York Times and featured on National Public Radio and CNN. One of his NPR interviews, titled "The Weird, Underappreciated World Of Plastic Packaging," explained that plastic packaging has become an integral part of the food system, and on CNN, he described how new plastics could prevent soft drinks from falling flat.
